questions.prompt: Who stands on the intended line to Navy2?
questions.explanation: Gold1 is between the carrier and Navy2 on the same line.

questions.prompt: Which actions can be explored under this activity rule?
questions.explanation: The briefing allows carrying or another pass. Availability still needs review.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to explore room away from the blocked line.
questions.explanation: This changes the angle to the options. It does not prove that Gold1 will stay fixed during a real carry.

questions.prompt: Arrange one response to a blocked plan.

options.text: Notice the lane has a defender
Choose after checking the new picture

questions.explanation: This avoids treating the first plan as an instruction that must be completed.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gold1 leaves Navy2's line while Navy2 stays available. Could Navy2 become an option again?

options.text: Yes, if a new check shows the lane is clear
Only if Navy2 first skates to a different spot
No, a first plan that gets blocked is finished for that shift

questions.explanation: Availability depends on the lane right now, not on a permanent label. Navy2 does not have to move for the lane to open, and a blocked first plan is not finished; what matters is what the next look shows.

questions.prompt: Why is changing your first plan sometimes useful?
questions.explanation: A relevant answer connects the changed lane with another visible option, while allowing more than one reasonable choice.

questions.prompt: Gold1 stays on the line to Navy2. Which option does this picture already offer?

options.text: A pass toward Navy3 on the other angle
A pass through Gold1 to Navy2
Waiting until Navy2's line opens on its own

questions.explanation: Navy3 stands on a different angle from the covered line to Navy2, so that is an option this picture offers, and the briefing also allows a short carry. A pass through Gold1 can give the opponent a chance to win the puck. Waiting can work if Gold1 is already leaving, but a still picture does not show that. Check the lane again before passing, because Navy3 can be covered as well.

questions.prompt: Which of these can YOU actually see in this picture?

options.text: Navy3 stands on a different angle from Navy2
Gold1 is already moving toward YOU

questions.explanation: The puck owner and the two navy angles are drawn in the picture. Nothing in a freeze shows a player moving, so Gold1's next move is not a fact yet.

questions.prompt: Move Navy3 to a spot that keeps a clear angle to YOU, away from the line Gold1 covers.
questions.explanation: This example gives Navy3 an angle that does not cross the line Gold1 covers, and it stays clear of Gold2. Other open spots work too; what matters is that YOU can see a lane Gold1 is not standing in.

questions.prompt: How can a covered lane still be useful information?
questions.explanation: Seeing Gold1 on the line to Navy2 tells YOU where the room is not, which points YOU toward Navy3 or toward a short carry. A good answer names what the covered lane told YOU, and accepts that the same lane can open again if Gold1 moves.

replacement.title: The other team has it now
replacement.objective: Update puck ownership and team roles after a loss.
replacement.briefing: Gold1 has just collected a lost puck in the small game. YOU and Navy2 are navy and no longer have possession. The earlier loss is stated, not animated. First identify the new picture before choosing a response. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: Gold1 is the new carrier.
Gold now has possession.
Gold2 is gold support.

questions.prompt: Which team has the puck now?
questions.explanation: Gold1, a gold player, owns the puck.

questions.prompt: Which players should YOU distinguish?
questions.explanation: Separate the actual carrier from their teammate rather than treating every opponent as a carrier.

questions.prompt: Arrange a simple reset after possession changes.

options.text: Choose a response with the coach's aim in mind

questions.explanation: This is an observation routine, not a sourced rule assigning every defender a specific threat.

questions.prompt: Find a place nearer the new play where YOU can still see Gold1 and Navy2.
questions.explanation: The reference changes the viewing and recovery relationship. No optimal defensive assignment is certified.

questions.prompt: Imagine Navy2 wins the puck back. What should YOU update first?
questions.explanation: The team roles change again when actual possession changes.

questions.prompt: What mistake could happen if you kept thinking YOU had the puck?
questions.explanation: You might plan a pass or shot you cannot make. Start from the actual carrier rather than the earlier state.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gold1 keeps the puck and skates toward the end navy defends. What comes first for YOU?

options.text: See where Gold1 is going and what ice is between Gold1 and that end
Get ready to receive a pass from Navy2
Skate straight to Gold2 and leave Gold1 to someone else

questions.explanation: Gold1 has the puck. Read the carrier, Gold2 and the space toward the navy end. Navy2 can help defend now, so check where your teammate is before choosing your route. If navy wins possession, update the read again.

questions.prompt: Which of these does the picture show right now?

options.text: Navy2 is across the ice on the other side from YOU
Gold2 is skating over to help Gold1

questions.explanation: The carrier and the two navy positions are drawn in the picture. A freeze shows no movement, so Gold2's next move is not a fact.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a spot between Gold1 and the end navy defends.
questions.explanation: This example puts YOU on the side of Gold1 that navy has to protect once gold has the puck. Gold2 is on that side as well, so check both before choosing. Another spot can work; what matters is that YOU can see the carrier and the ice between Gold1 and that end.

questions.prompt: Navy2 is across the ice from YOU. How can that change what YOU watch and what Navy2 watches?
questions.explanation: Two navy players on different sides can cover different ice instead of following the same opponent. A good answer names one thing YOU would watch and one thing YOU would leave to Navy2, and accepts that both change if Gold1 turns the other way.

replacement.title: Face the play while moving back

replacement.briefing: The coach says YOU are practising moving backward toward the defending end while facing the attacking end. The picture is a freeze, not a moving trace. Gold1 carries the puck toward YOU; Navy2 waits behind and to one side. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: YOU face the attacking end.
The stated exercise moves YOU toward the defending end.
Gold1 is ahead of the facing direction.

questions.prompt: Which way does the coach say YOU are moving?
questions.explanation: This comes from the stated exercise. The static picture does not independently show velocity.

questions.prompt: Which player is ahead of the way YOU face?
questions.explanation: Gold1 is ahead of YOU, in the direction YOU face.

questions.prompt: What can this exercise ask you to notice?
questions.explanation: You can discuss the visible play. The display does not measure physical skating.

questions.prompt: Show another practice position a little farther back while facing the play.
questions.explanation: This matches the stated movement direction. It is not a universal defensive gap or proof that the skate is feasible.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gold1 changes direction. What could you do before another movement?

options.text: Keep moving because the first plan never changes

questions.explanation: Update the cue. The correct physical transition needs on-ice instruction and a validated trace.

questions.prompt: What is different about facing a direction and moving in that direction?
questions.explanation: A player can face the play while moving backward. Use the stated exercise rather than guessing motion from a still image.

questions.prompt: Gold1 gets too close for comfortable backward movement. What could help in this practice?

options.text: Turn and skate to regain room while checking Gold1
Stay backward even if Gold1 goes past
Reach with the stick and stop moving

questions.explanation: A controlled turn can help regain room. The coach should teach and observe that movement on ice; there is no fixed gap that fits every skater.

questions.prompt: What should YOU check when turning to move back faster?

options.text: Where Gold1 and the puck are going
Whether the route behind is clear of Navy2
Only how quickly YOU can turn

questions.explanation: Keep track of the carrier and the space you are moving into. Speed alone does not tell you whether the route is useful or clear.

questions.prompt: Move Navy2 to a waiting spot behind YOU that leaves the straight retreat lane clear.
questions.explanation: This keeps Navy2 to one side of YOUR path toward the defending end. The actual skating route still depends on how Gold1 moves.

questions.prompt: How could Navy2 help YOU notice space behind without taking over your looking?
questions.explanation: Navy2 can give a short call about their location or a clear route. YOU still check while moving; a call adds information and does not replace looking.

replacement.title: The blocked pass is loose
replacement.objective: Distinguish a pass attempt from completed reception.
replacement.briefing: A pass from Navy2 was deflected and now lies loose between the players. This picture begins after the deflection; no path is animated. YOU have not collected it yet. Gold1 is nearby and Navy2 remains available. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: The pass did not reach a controlled receiver.
The puck has no owner.
Both teams can see the loose puck.

questions.prompt: Did the pass finish with YOU controlling it?

options.text: Yes, YOU have it on your stick
No, the puck is loose between the players
Yes, because the pass was meant for YOU

questions.explanation: The briefing and setup identify a loose puck between the players, not a completed reception. A pass aimed at YOU still has to be collected before YOU can use it.

questions.prompt: Which facts are present now?

options.text: YOU already made the next shot

questions.explanation: A loose puck and a nearby opponent are shown; a next shot is not.

questions.prompt: Order the supplied puck events.

options.text: It is loose at this freeze

questions.explanation: This is declared history. The earlier path is not simulated.

questions.prompt: Show a nearby place from which YOU could approach the loose puck.
questions.explanation: This moves toward the puck without claiming who will reach it first. Check other players before a real approach.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gold1 controls it first. Which plan needs to change?

options.text: A plan to shoot it yourself immediately

questions.explanation: YOU cannot perform a puck action while Gold1 controls it. Update possession before choosing.

questions.prompt: Why is an attempted pass different from a completed pass?
questions.explanation: A pass can be deflected or stay loose. Control by the receiver must actually happen.

questions.prompt: If Gold1 controls the loose puck first, which responses could help Navy defend?

options.text: Protect a useful route toward the navy net
Keep waiting in the old passing spot
Find Navy2 so you can cover different space

questions.explanation: Possession has changed. Read Gold1 and the route to your net, then use Navy2’s location to avoid both chasing the same space.

questions.prompt: Which statements does the briefing actually tell us?

options.text: YOU have not collected the puck

questions.explanation: The deflection and lack of a controlled reception are stated. The briefing does not say who touched the pass.

questions.prompt: Move Navy2 closer to YOU to offer support if YOU collect the puck.
questions.explanation: This example brings Navy2 closer on a different angle. If YOU gain control and the lane stays clear, Navy2 could offer a short pass back. Keep checking Gold1; another support spot may work.

questions.prompt: After YOU collect it, why might a pass back to Navy2 help against Gold2 ahead?
questions.explanation: Navy2 offers support behind YOU, away from Gold2’s side. If the lane is clear, a pass back can keep possession and create a new angle. Check Gold1 too before using it.

replacement.title: Two players crowd the puck
replacement.objective: Notice concentrated pressure and offer a different support angle.
replacement.briefing: Navy2 has the puck. Both Gold1 and Gold2 are close to Navy2 from the goalward side. YOU are farther to one side; Navy3 waits on the other side. The activity allows a short outlet or a carry if space exists. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: Two gold players are near Navy2.
Navy2 is the current carrier.
YOU and Navy3 are separate support players.

questions.explanation: YOU and Navy3 are teammates without possession. Gold1 is an opponent.

questions.prompt: Explore another outlet angle behind the concentrated pressure.
questions.explanation: The reference changes the passing relationship to Navy2. It suggests an available area, not a safe route to reach it or a guaranteed pass.

questions.prompt: Arrange one support response to this crowding.
questions.explanation: This is one suggested response. Navy2 may have another reasonable action.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gold2 leaves Navy2 to cover YOU. What should you notice?

options.text: Both the new cover and Navy2's changed space
Only that your first spot was good

questions.explanation: An opponent moving away changes more than one relationship.

questions.prompt: How might helping Navy2 differ from skating beside Navy2?
questions.explanation: Support can be an available angle outside the crowd. Discuss alternatives without treating one reference point as uniquely correct.

questions.prompt: If Gold2 shifts across to Gold1's side of Navy2, which space could open?

options.text: The side Gold2 left, if YOU can get there and be seen
A lane straight through both gold players
No new space, because Navy2 is still in the crowd

questions.explanation: Pressure that gathers on one side leaves more room on the other. That room only helps if Navy2 can see YOU and the lane is clear, so check both before calling for the puck. If Gold2 turns back, the picture changes again.

questions.prompt: Which two things are true in this freeze?

options.text: Gold1 and Gold2 are on different sides across the width of the ice
Navy3 is calling for the puck

questions.explanation: The carrier and the two gold positions are drawn in the picture. A still picture carries no sound, so what Navy3 is saying is not shown.

questions.prompt: Move Navy3 to a support spot on the opposite side from YOU, behind the two gold players.
questions.explanation: This example puts Navy3 on a different angle from YOU. Gold1 is near the puck, so Navy2 must check the defender and the passing lane before using either option. Another clear support spot may work.

questions.prompt: What could tell YOU that your support spot is no longer useful?
questions.explanation: A gold player stepping into your lane, or Navy2 turning away from your side, both change the answer. A good answer names one cue YOU would watch for and one thing YOU would do next, and accepts that Navy3's spot matters as well.

replacement.title: Our half-ice change signal
replacement.objective: Recognize the puck-release and change routine in a named game model.
replacement.briefing: This activity uses the Hockey Canada U9 half-ice change rule: on the designated change signal, release the puck and leave for the next unit while play continues. The signal has just sounded while YOU control the puck. The full-rink picture shows player relationships only, not the exact half-ice layout or bench. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: The designated change signal was stated.
YOU still own the puck at this instant.
The next unit waits off the illustrated area.

questions.prompt: Who must release the puck at this instant?

options.text: Gold1, the gold player up ice
Navy2, once YOU pass it there first

questions.explanation: YOU are the declared puck owner when the change signal sounds. The named routine asks the carrier to let go of the puck right away, not to move it to a teammate first.

questions.prompt: Which instructions belong to this named routine?

options.text: Let go of the puck right away
Finish a long attack before changing

questions.explanation: Those actions follow the quoted model in the briefing. Local program applicability still needs review.

questions.prompt: Arrange the declared change sequence.

options.text: The next unit continues the activity

questions.explanation: This describes the model, not a moving trace or a universal rule for all games.

questions.prompt: Does the whole game stop for this stated change?

options.text: Yes, the official stops play for a faceoff
Yes, everyone waits until the new players are on

questions.explanation: The briefing states that play continues in this half-ice model. The new players come on while the puck is still live.

questions.prompt: Imagine a different practice says whistle means stop and listen. Which instruction applies there?

options.text: Whatever the other players happen to do

questions.explanation: Signals need context. A practice stop and this game change routine are different.

questions.prompt: How can you know which whistle routine the coach is using?
questions.explanation: Listen to the activity instructions and ask if unclear. The scenario does not establish a rule for every U9 program.

questions.prompt: For the next branch, imagine Gold1 reaches the puck after YOU release it. In this change routine, what should YOU do?

options.text: Continue leaving for the next unit
Chase Gold1 to win it back first
Stay until Navy2 gets the puck

questions.explanation: The designated signal still means release and change in this named activity. A new puck owner does not cancel the change instruction.

questions.prompt: What helps the next unit take its turn in this activity?

options.text: Release the puck when the change signal sounds
Leave using the route the coach explained
Take the puck with YOU to the waiting players

questions.explanation: Release control and make room for the next unit. Use the real activity’s exit route; the picture does not show the bench.

questions.prompt: The picture does not show the bench or the waiting area. What does it show right now?

options.text: Where Navy2 and Gold1 stand at this instant
The exact route to the waiting area
How much time is left in this shift

questions.explanation: The illustration gives player positions at this instant and nothing else. It has no bench, no route and no clock, so ask your coach for the real change route.

questions.prompt: Why should YOU leave after the signal even when the attacking end is nearby?
questions.explanation: In this named half-ice routine, the signal gives the next unit its turn while play continues. Being near the attacking end does not mean finishing another attack first. Other game formats can use different routines.

replacement.title: Make room after the goalie whistle

Gold1 now has restart possession.
YOU are about two metres from the restart puck, inside the three-metre cushion.
The crease is near the gold goal.

questions.prompt: What should YOU pay attention to before resuming?

options.text: An automatic faceoff after every hold

questions.explanation: Follow the named model and the actual signal rather than importing another game's restart.

questions.prompt: Why do you need to give Gold1 room before play continues?

questions.prompt: Gold1 starts moving with the restart puck while YOU are still backing away. What guides YOUR next action?

options.text: The official’s restart instruction for this activity

questions.prompt: During the retreat, what should YOU keep track of?

questions.prompt: Which net does gold attack in this activity?

questions.prompt: Why should a whistle make you reset your read?
questions.explanation: The puck may be in a new place and a different player may control the next action. Resetting prevents carrying an old plan into a changed activity.

questions.prompt: Gold1 closes on Navy2. What is the most useful thing YOU can do?

options.text: Offer a clear short outlet Navy2 can reach
Skate as far from Navy2 as YOU can
Hold your spot and let Navy2 solve it alone

questions.explanation: Under pressure a nearby clear outlet is often easier to use than the farthest spot on the ice. Navy3 offers a wider option from the other side, so if YOUR lane is covered, moving to a different open spot is the better help.

questions.prompt: Why is spacing about help, not distance alone?
questions.explanation: YOU need enough separation to give Navy2 room, but still need to be visible and reachable. The pressure on the carrier and Navy3's option from the other side of the ice shape the best choice.
